planting.note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in late winter or very early spring, since this first-early pea needs a long cool stretch to fill its large pods before summer heat arrives.

directions: Sow seed about an inch deep in cool, well-drained soil as early as the ground can be worked, since Gradus is a first-early wrinkled pea bred to mature quickly in cold weather. Provide brush, netting, or a low trellis for the three-to-four-foot vines, which otherwise sprawl and tangle. This English Victorian-era variety, associated with the nurseryman Thomas Laxton, was long valued for pods as large and well-filled as main-crop types despite ripening weeks earlier, making it a favorite for both the table and the show bench. Pick pods promptly once plump, since flavor and sweetness fade quickly as the peas mature past their prime.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange heirloom pea records

planting.note: Direct sow in cool soil a few weeks before the last frost; the tall vines of this 1860s English heirloom need sturdy netting or brush support from an early stage.

directions: Sow directly in cool, fertile soil and install support early, as Yorkshire Hero climbs tall and tangles badly without it. First grown in England around the 1860s and widely listed in British and North American seed catalogs through the late nineteenth century, it produces creamy white, deeply wrinkled seeds prized in their green stage for a delicate, sweet flavor. The variety fell out of commercial favor as newer dwarf and disease-resistant peas took over the market, and it now survives mainly through heritage seed-saving networks. Pick regularly once pods fill out, since this older type holds its quality less long on the vine than modern hybrids.

planting.note: Direct sow in cool soil well before the last frost; this tall Victorian exhibition pea needs a sturdy trellis or fence from the start to support its long vines.

directions: Direct sow in cool, well-drained soil and provide tall support immediately, since this nineteenth-century English heirloom climbs four to five feet and produces exceptionally long, well-filled pods. Duke of Albany belongs to the same Victorian lineage of large-podded exhibition peas as Telegraph and Stratagem, grown both for the table and for competitive showing in its day. It has been preserved in cultivation by heritage seed organizations after disappearing from mainstream commercial catalogs. Harvest pods while still glossy and full for the sweetest flavor, as older, drier pods lose tenderness quickly.

planting.note: Direct sow in cool soil ahead of the last frost; this dwarf, large-podded Victorian pea stays shorter than many main-crop types but still benefits from light brush support.

directions: Sow directly in cool, well-drained soil in early spring; Stratagem stays relatively compact for an heirloom marrowfat pea, but its unusually large, dark blue-green pods still benefit from a low brush or netting support to keep them off the ground. First described in English horticultural literature around 1880 as a dwarf wrinkled marrow selected from the old Telegraph pea strain, it was prized in its day both as a late-season table pea and as an exhibition variety for its outsized pods. Pick pods while they remain plump and glossy for the best flavor and texture, since this older type sweetens less in storage than modern varieties.
